title: $20,000 Donation to Rural Aid to Support Aussie Farmers
author: Aaron
body:
In the early hours of the morning on 30th December 2019, an uncontrollable blaze swept through a family farm near Cudgewa in northeast Victoria, leaving a path of devastation in its wake.

Lynne, a staff member of the APT Travel Group (ATG), grew up on a farm near the Snowy Mountains, a farm which has been owned by her family for four generations. Stretching across over 400 hectares of both hill and flat country, the farm was home to woolly sheep grazing on the hills, while bellowing cattle took up residence along the flats.

2019 marked the beginning of Australia’s worst bushfire season to date. More than 7.3 million hectares of land was destroyed, including Lynne’s family’s farm. Already on high alert after the fire warnings, Lynne, who was staying at the farm at the time, was able to transport her family to safety before the fires hit. Meanwhile, her brother and father stayed behind to courageously defend their home.

Their tenacity and strength saved the family home, the shearing shed and the machinery shed. However, the rest of the farm was completely obliterated. 95% of the land was burnt and blackened, almost all fences were destroyed, the old dairy gone, the original farm homestead was ruined along with irreplaceable photos, furniture and mementos, and a third of their beautiful animals had lost their lives.

Lynne’s father and brother were lucky to escape with their lives. It was a miracle both came out of the fight with no more than singed eyelids and superficial burns. However, leaving a scar are the memories of the moment when the fire hit.

The aftermath has proved even more of a hardship. The rest of the community were tending to their own destroyed properties, so Lynne and her family were on their own. Water supplies were polluted by the smoke, surviving livestock were severely traumatised, and all pasture grass had been burnt, so there was no food for the animals.

Lynne recalls the first moment she was able to drive into the farm once the smoke had cleared. “It felt like someone was squeezing my heart. The destruction the fire caused is not something I can describe except to say, everything was so very black.”

Fast forwarding five months on, the farm is starting to come back to life. After some decent rainfall, green has begun to sprout. Some pasture grasses have recovered, and after receiving a hay donation from Rural Aid, the livestock have food to eat.

In May 2020, OneTomorrow made a $20,000 donation to Rural Aid, who will be using a portion of this donation to support Lynne and her family through this difficult time.

“The amount of work that we have done so far is enormous. The amount of work still to do is unbelievable,” says Lynne. Weeks upon weeks have been spent repairing the fences, with no end in sight. Lynne’s father, at 79 years of age, has shown a tremendous effort to return his farm to its former glory. In the months since the fires hit, he has had only two days of rest. He, like many other farmers in a similar situation, will receive much-needed support from Rural Aid, which will play a part in the immense task of getting the farm back on track.

The kindness shown by complete strangers helps spur Lynne and her family on. “I would like to take this opportunity to thank OneTomorrow and all the ATG staff who support OneTomorrow, who have shown such generosity to my family,” says Lynne.
